course_description:
Two dimensional kinematics and kinetics of particles and rigid bodies; Applications of work energy and impulse momentum methods; Vibration of single degree of freedom systems; Balancing of rotating masses.

MECH2210 is the first dedicated dynamics course for mechanical, aerospace and mechatronic engineering students. It develops the ability to model, analyse and solve engineering dynamics problems of two-dimensional systems. The course emphasises not only procedural problem-solving but the development of engineering judgement- understanding of the assumptions underpinning a model, when those assumptions are valid, and how to approach problems that do not arrive in textbook form. This prepares students for more advance study in MECH3200 and for professional practice where dynamically generated forces and motions are central to design and analysis.

course_aims: In this course, you will learn the fundamental principles, tools and methods essential for analysing the dynamics of engineering systems. By the end of the course, you will have developed the ability to model and analyse the planar (two-dimensional) motion of engineering systems and assess the assumptions underlying dynamic models.

learning_outcomes.description: Kinematics. Describe and analyse motion of particles and 2D rigid bodies using Cartesian, normal-tangential and polar coordinate systems, and apply relative motion and instantaneous centre of rotation (ICR) methods to determine velocities and acceleration in constrained systems.

Kinetics. Formulate Newton-Euler equations to derive and solve equations of motion for particles and 2D rigid bodies, including systems with constraints and coupled bodies, construct Free Body Diagrams (FBDs) and Kinetic Diagrams, calculate mass moments of inertia, and interpret the resulting motion in physical terms

Work-energy methods. Apply principle of work-energy to describe particle and 2D rigid body linear/angular motion, differentiate between conservative and nonconservative forces, and calculate instantaneous power and mechanical efficiency in engineering systems.

Impulse-momentum methods. Use linear and angular impulse-momentum principles to analyse particle dynamics and 2D rigid body motion, to solve problems involving collision and varying mass, and select appropriately between Newton-Euler, energy and momentum methods for a given problem

Single degree of freedom vibration. Derive and solve equations of motion for free, forced, undamped and damped single degree of freedom systems, interpret frequency response and vibration transmissibility in the context of isolation and measurement applications.

Balancing of rotating machinery and eccentric excitation. Derive conditions for static and dynamic balance of rotating systems, calculate corrective masses and their positioning, evaluate system response due to eccentric excitation including bearing forces due to an imbalance.
Modelling Assumptions and Engineering Judgement. Identify and critically evaluate the assumptions underlying Newtonian dynamic models, and recognise when a problem requires more advanced analysis.

Transfer and Application to Novel Problems. Analyse the dynamics of unfamiliar engineering systems by selecting appropriate models and methods, constructing and solving equations of motion, and interpreting results in physical and engineering terms

assessment_details.task_description: Weekly online quiz using the Pearson “Mastering Engineering” platform. This platform integrates into Blackboard and enables the course to run assessed quizzes which draw from a large range of example dynamics problems. The problems are randomisable to ensure all students work with a unique set of numbers to ensure individual work in support of academic integrity. The maximum mark for each week's quiz is 1.9% of the overall course grade. There are 12 quizzes in total that will run from weeks 2-13. The total mark for this assessment item is calculated at the end of semester by adding up your best 10 results across the 12 quizzes in the semester You are required to register with Pearson Mastering in Week 1 of Semester so that you are able to complete the assessed online quizzes. If you encounter technical problems doing so, as a first step you should refer to the provided support documents on Blackboard; as a second step, seek advice through the Ed Discussion Board; if you continue to have problems you should contact the Course Coordinator by email. If you leave the registration process until Week 2 and encounter technical problems which prevent submission of your quiz by the due date, these technical problems will not be accepted as grounds for an extension to the assessment. Please note, the Mastering website will periodically be unavailable due to planned maintenance. This typically occurs over a finite number of hours on a weekend day. We will normally provide advance notice of this, and in such cases we expect students to plan their website access around these times. Failure to do so will not be considered an excuse for late submission. Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.title: Practical laboratory work
assessment_details.task_description: During the semester, you will complete three laboratory tasks that are directly related to the content covered in lectures and practical assignments. Each of these tasks is based around a worksheet, which you can download from the course's Blackboard site. During practical classes students work in small groups and complete a worksheet (one worksheet per group). During the practical sessions, casual academics will be available to assist you with using the experimental equipment and to help clarify the concepts you are learning. Students who experience challenges with their laboratory team can access resources online here . Teams unable to resolve their challenges should reach out to the immediate teaching team for assistance. Criteria and Marking: Assessment will be based on a casual academic's observations of each group's participation in the practical and understanding of the concepts covered. Casual Academics will assign each group a mark of 0, 1, or 2 in each practical based on the following criteria: 0 - The group did not actively participate in the practical and/or demonstrate sufficient understanding. 1 - The group participated in the practical, completed most the work and demonstrated some (but not full) understanding of the concepts involved through answers to the worksheet questions, engaging effectively as a team to do so 2 - The group participated in the practical, completed the work and demonstrated an understanding of the concepts involved through answers to the worksheet questions, engaging effectively as a team to do so. Casual Academics will progressively mark each group during the practical using the practical worksheet and provide feedback on responses. Completed worksheets will be archived by the responsible casual academic, who will record marks obtained by each group against the group members' names. Each student is responsible for ensuring that their name is recorded on the group worksheet. Each student is encouraged to complete an individual copy of the worksheet during the practical for their own records. Read full task description Hide full task description
